documents.abstract: This workshop shares the experience of building a deep phenotyping dataset of music-evoked emotions, namely "ManyMusic🎶" (). This ongoing project involves 17 EEG sessions and 17 fMRI sessions per participant, measuring neural and behavioural responses during intense affective experiences evoked by complete musical works spanning a wide range of genres, including Western classical, jazz, rock, pop, hip-hop, and more. Across six participants, the project will collect data from more than 1,000 full-length musical pieces.In this workshop, we will discuss the challenges of building a deep phenotyping dataset such as stimulus selection, participant screening, data quality monitoring, and on-the-fly troubleshooting. Participants will also have the opportunity to examine a subset of the collected EEG data first-hand. We will conclude by discussing the future prospects of developing foundation models from deeply sampled multimodal datasets.

The Internet of Things (IoT) links sensors, machines, vehicles and everyday objects so that they can exchange data and act with little human intervention. Fifth-generation (5G) networks introduced dedicated support for massive machine-type and ultra-reliable low-latency communication, but emerging applications such as autonomous transport, remote surgery, immersive extended reality and large-scale digital twins demand still higher data rates, lower latency, greater reliability, precise positioning and far denser connectivity. Sixth-generation (6G) networks, now being defined under the IMT-2030 framework, aim to meet these needs and to make artificial intelligence a native part of the network. This survey reviews 6G-enabled IoT. It summarises the requirements and key performance indicators, and explains the enabling technologies: terahertz and sub-terahertz communication, intelligent reflecting surfaces, integrated sensing and communication, edge intelligence, AI-native network management and non-terrestrial networks. A five-layer architecture for 6G-enabled IoT is presented, linking devices, access, edge, core and applications under a cross-layer security and energy plane. Applications in smart cities, connected vehicles, healthcare, industrial automation, precision agriculture and environmental monitoring are discussed. Finally, open challenges including infrastructure cost, spectrum regulation, energy consumption, security and privacy, and the management of billions of devices are identified.

In computer vision, object detection and recognition processes are used to identify and locate objects in images. Humans can recognize a wide range of things in photos with little effort, even if the images vary somewhat from different angles, sizes, and scales, or when they are moved or rotated. Objects can be identified even when partially blocked from vision. This task remains a challenge for computer vision systems. Several approaches to the task have been implemented over the years. In many computer vision systems, the first duty is object detection, which allows us to learn more about the identified object and the scene. Researchers have recently focused their emphasis on the application of Machine learning techniques. Machine learning uses multiple layers to separate raw information into higher-level features. This paper outlines a recommended research methodology. This method uses a convolutional neural network-based architecture with a limited amount of data to detect objects in an image. The data used is the MAR database, and the process classifies thirty images into four distinct classes with high accuracy. The approaches outlined in this research included data collection and pre-processing, as well as designing and developing a hardwarebased machine learning system. This study discusses the many techniques to object identification, their similarities, the limitations of existing work, and, finally, the model given in the last section of the paper.
topics: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

documents.abstract: Background Children with Down syndrome (DS) often experience delays in gross motor development due to hypotonia and motor coordination deficits, which can limit their participation in physical activities. Traditional assessments of motor performance are mainly subjective and may lack consistency across evaluators. Integrating artificial intelligence and computer vision into educational settings presents an opportunity to enhance the objectivity, precision, and scalability of such assessments. This study presents the development and evaluation of an automated system that utilizes pose estimation and machine learning to classify gross motor performance in children with Down syndrome, to support inclusive physical education practices. Methods We recruited 23 children with DS (aged 4–10) from educational institutions affiliated with Cáritas Arequipa, Peru. Participants performed four standardized gross motor exercises: two-footed jumps, ball toss, crawling, and sit-to-stand transitions. High-resolution Canon cameras recorded the movements, and the MediaPipe Holistic framework was used to extract 33 key body landmarks per frame. From these data, spatiotemporal features were computed and reduced using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to minimize dimensionality while preserving variance. Expert evaluators labeled each exercise attempt into one of three performance categories: high, moderate, or low. Five supervised machine learning algorithms—Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN), and Logistic Regression—were trained and compared using a stratified 80/20 train-test split. Model performance was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, accuracy, and Cohen’s Kappa coefficient. Results All classifiers achieved high accuracy (>93%). The Random Forest model yielded the most balanced and robust results, with an overall accuracy of 95.55%, macro-average F1-score of 0.96, and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.933, indicating near-perfect agreement with expert labels. Logistic Regression showed slightly higher accuracy (95.79%) but was less effective at modeling nonlinear patterns. Notably, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) on the first principal component (PC1) revealed significant differences between performance classes (F(2, 9,123) = 62.98, p = 7.00 × 10 −28 , η² = 0.0143), confirming PC1 as a discriminative metric for motor performance. Misclassifications occurred primarily between adjacent categories ( e.g ., moderate vs . high), with minimal confusion between high and low classes. Conclusions The proposed system demonstrates strong potential as an objective and scalable solution for monitoring gross motor skills in children with DS using low-cost hardware and open-source tools. Its integration into educational settings may help personalize instruction and support inclusive physical education by providing real-time, data-informed feedback to educators.
topics: Down syndrome and intellectual disability research

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) facilitates access to information in education, increasing the importance of critically evaluating claims and their underlying assumptions. This study examined Grade 10 students’ ability to distinguish facts, opinions, and values in AI-related information at SMA Don Bosco Padang from a philosophy of science perspective. A descriptive quantitative approach was employed involving 33 students. Data were collected through a 15-item written test comprising five items each for fact, opinion, and value identification. Descriptive analysis examined frequencies, percentages of correct responses, score distributions, and classification error patterns. Across 495 responses, 337 were correct and 158 were incorrect, yielding an overall accuracy of 68.08%. Accuracy was highest for opinion identification (76.36%), followed by fact identification (67.88%) and value identification (60.00%). Value identification presented the greatest difficulty, with an error rate of 40.00%. These findings reveal descriptive differences in students’ classification performance, particularly their greater difficulty recognizing values within AI-related information. From a philosophy of science perspective, the results underscore the relevance of epistemology for evaluating evidence and the justification of claims, alongside axiology for recognizing ethical considerations. The study provides contextual evidence to inform AI literacy instruction that integrates information verification, critical reasoning, and ethical reflection to support responsible technology use.

Explainable machine learning has been applied to textual predictors of writing quality, but rarely to the behavioral and motivational predictors, feedback modality and self-regulated learning (SRL), that dominate confirmatory EFL writing research. This study analyzes a quasi-experimental, ten-week EFL writing-feedback intervention (n=84), recording feedback condition (instructor-mediated, automated, or generative-AI), proficiency, and 35-item SRL strategy use alongside pre/post analytic writing scores across six outcomes. A pre-modeling reliability check found the SRL questionnaire did not reproduce its published factor structure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.279), so a single composite served as the motivational predictor, with centered feedback-by-SRL interaction terms. Five model classes were compared under nested cross-validation with per-trait tuning. Random forest achieved the best aggregate performance (MCRMSE = 2.240, mean R² = 0.293); a stacked ensemble performed worse than its base learners on every trait (mean R² = −0.344). A fixed-hyperparameter baseline outperformed the nested-CV-tuned pipeline (MCRMSE 2.197 vs. 2.258), showing tuning, not feature engineering, degraded performance here. SHAP attribution identified feedback condition, especially generative-AI feedback, as the dominant predictor for all six outcomes, with feedback-by-SRL interactions outweighing SRL's own main effect on three of six traits. A multi-task neural network outperformed an equivalent single-task ensemble on every trait using 5.75 times fewer parameters. These results show explainable, cross-validated machine learning can corroborate confirmatory EFL writing findings while surfacing measurement and methodological cautions.

Ergonomic workstation design is essential for improving the fit between workers, tasks, and the work environment while reducing the risk of work-related musculoskeletal disorders. The Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS) is widely used for ergonomic risk assessment; however, its conventional application to dynamic work can be inefficient because numerous working postures must be observed and evaluated. Moreover, conventional ergonomic design often requires multiple physical mock-ups, while motion-capture technologies such as Kinect are generally applied to existing work conditions, limiting their use for preventive evaluation during the design stage. This study proposes a digital ergonomics framework integrating workstation modeling, work-process simulation, and OWAS-based risk assessment for preventive ergonomic optimization. Digital models of the workstation and work activities were developed to simulate worker postures and identify potentially hazardous conditions before physical implementation. OWAS was used to classify postural risks and determine the required corrective actions. Workstation configurations and work procedures associated with higher risk levels were iteratively modified and reassessed in the digital environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can identify and reduce ergonomic risks during the design stage without extensive physical prototyping. Higher-risk postures were mitigated through iterative modifications of workstation configurations and work procedures. This framework provides a systematic preventive approach for integrating ergonomic assessment into workstation and work-process design, supporting safer working conditions while improving the efficiency of the ergonomic design process
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study develops an extended Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model that integrates innovation, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital transformation into a macroeconomic framework for Vietnam. The model employs a parsimonious, single-channel architecture: three forms of rival capital (physical, digital, and AI) enter a single production function, while a non-rival knowledge stock drives endogenous total factor productivity. Calibrated using Vietnamese aggregate evidence and policy anchors for 2000–2024, supplemented by international proxy ranges, the model shows that sustained, institutionally supported investment in AI and digital transformation can raise long-run output and welfare. The magnitude of these conditional gains is moderate and depends strongly on institutional quality and public spending, while remaining quantitatively sensitive to selected knowledge and policy parameters. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation offer opportunities to improve productivity and living standards in Vietnam. Using an economic model calibrated to Vietnamese macroeconomic evidence for 2000–2024, this study explores alternative investment scenarios. The simulations suggest that sustained investment can raise output and aggregate welfare, with gains depending on institutional capacity to convert public spending into productive knowledge. For policymakers, the implications are to strengthen project selection, accountable implementation, data governance and workforce skills alongside investment, and to phase expenditure according to implementation capacity. Reskilling and support for affected workers matter because aggregate gains do not ensure equal benefits across groups. These are conditional simulations using calibrated AI and digital capital stocks, not forecasts or direct estimates of realised economic effects. The framework can inform policy appraisal and public debate on how technology investment and institutional reform can jointly support Vietnam’s long-term development.

Abstract Just-in-Time (JIT) software defect prediction tries to flag risky commits the moment they are committed, before they can cause problems in a codebase. Most existing approaches rely on simple change metrics, such as how many lines were added or how experienced the developer is, but these numbers say very little about what a change actually does. This paper presents a hybrid framework that looks at a commit from three angles at once: traditional change metrics, a semantic understanding of the code from CodeBERT, and structured reasoning about intent and risk generated by a large language model. We built a multi-language dataset of nearly 60,000 commits from 19 open-source Java, Python, and C/C++ projects, and tested several ways of combining these three sources of information using standard machine learning classifiers. Combining traditional metrics with CodeBERT's code understanding consistently gave the strongest results, clearly outperforming any single source used alone. Adding the LLM-based reasoning on top of that combination did not meaningfully improve things further, though it was genuinely useful when paired with either of the other two sources on its own. Overall, our results suggest that combining structural and semantic information is a practical way to catch defects early, while a third, coarser reasoning layer adds little once the first two are already working together.

Automated ergonomic exposure and risk assessments, leveraging measures from wearable sensors and markerless motion capture systems, is being increasingly adopted in manual material handling contexts as an alternative to self-reports and direct observation. Machine learning and artificial intelligence (ML/AI) algorithms trained on these measures enable continuous estimation of musculoskeletal demands and injury risk; however, model accuracy and generalizability remain constrained when training datasets lack diversity in worker characteristics and task conditions. In particular, insufficient representation of demographic factors and load-handling scenarios can lead to biased or non-generalizable models. Existing open-access, occupational movement datasets rarely capture such variability, often relying on small, homogeneous samples and single load types. To address these limitations, we present a cloud-based, public database comprising data from 40 participants (20 male, 20 female), including younger adults [mean (SD) age = 23 (3.1) years] and older adults [55.5 (5.3) years], who performed simulated occupational lifting/lowering and pushing/pulling tasks. Data were collected from three sensing modalities—inertial measurement units (IMUs), markerless motion capture (Kinect), and an electromyography (EMG) armband—using multiple load configurations, load masses (2.3-11.3 kg), lifting heights, and handling depths. This database supports the development, benchmarking, and cross-modal evaluation of ML/AI algorithms for ergonomic exposure and risk assessments in occupational settings.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder with diverse and complex manifestations. This condition requires early detection which is crucial in finding a cure. Traditional diagnostic procedures are biased and time-consuming. These create a pressing need for objective and accessible screening tools. The rapid development of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning (DL) methods, offers promising resolutions for automating ASD detection. Such detection is done through analyzing behavioral and physical biomarkers. This study proposes a convenient but complex neural network to support early ASD screening through facial images. The model classifies facial images of children as autistic or non-autistic by using the publicly available Autistic Children Facial Dataset. Various experiments assess the model’s performance. The design is developed to be statistically efficient, which makes it suitable for mobile and embedded systems for real-time screening. Results show that our proposed model shows better performance than the existing approaches, especially in the levels of accuracy and area under curve (AUC). This further confirms its efficiency and prospects for autism screening applications. Achieving accuracy of 98.97%, the model delivers better performance than the evaluated benchmark models. These findings affirm that lightweight image-focused DL approaches are well suited to provide clinicians with a trustworthy and scalable method for early ASD screening. Thus, it is evident that the proposed model facilitates timely support for individuals and families.

People converse with AI as they would with friends in daily life, collaborate with it, and form personalized relationships. In response to these emerging forms of interaction, this study clarifies the concept of Human-Friendly Interaction with conversational AI and develops the Human-Friendly AI Interaction Design Framework (HFAI-DF). This study positions anthropomorphism, a foundational phenomenon in human–AI interaction, as a theoretical bridge and reviews literature on anthropomorphism theory and related research on human cognition. On this basis, this study interpretively derives and organizes how anthropomorphism-inducing stimuli can be applied to AI agents, systematizing them into 30 AI behavioral items that enable human-friendly interaction. Subsequently, a survey was conducted and exploratory factor analysis performed to identify six dimensions as a preliminary structure for a design framework for AI’s human-friendly interaction. These dimensions are: Self-Aware Interaction, User-Adaptive Responsiveness Interaction, Context-Aware Reasoning Interaction, Socio-Emotional Interaction, Creative Collaboration Interaction, and Proactive Assistance Interaction. Within the evolving AI research landscape focused on interaction, this study extends the human-centered AI concept toward human-friendly interaction that operates in an organic manner comparable to human–human conversation, grounded in an understanding of human cognitive functioning. The proposed framework provides both AI providers and designers with an initial structure for shaping and improving the quality of human-friendly interaction.

documents.abstract: This systematic review critically analyzes the contexts and challenges of Levels of Automation (LOA), particularly in light of advancements by Artificial Intelligence (AI). Human–automation interaction (HAI) seeks to understand how humans interact with automated systems, particularly as increasing automation places operators increasingly out of the loop. A foundational framework within this field is the Levels of Automation (LOA) framework, which characterizes the respective roles and capabilities of human operators and automated systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into traditional HAI applications, a renewed examination of the current state of LOA is warranted. This systematic review examines the following research question: What research demographics, contexts, and challenges associated with LOA are reported in the literature? Data analysis, extraction, and open and axial coding were employed, and consensus was reached by iterative discussion between the authors. The review ultimately included 118 studies. The review identified six contextual categories and 26 challenge codes. The findings provide a comprehensive analysis of the evolving landscape of human–automation interaction. The contribution of this work is to outline weaknesses embedded in research with LOA and suggest a reform with prospects of enhanced HAI with AI.

This systematic review synthesizes 15 empirical studies published in 2026 to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is affecting Iranian education and what the current evidence supports. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a search of four databases yielded 710 records, of which 15 empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in a thematic synthesis. The corpus comprises twelve journal articles and three chapters in edited volumes. The synthesis identified four themes. The first is that GenAI is effective when it is paired with human mediation and less effective when it replaces it, a finding that is replicated across every study in the corpus that compared AI-only and hybrid conditions. The second is that the benefits of GenAI are unevenly distributed across linguistic domains, with stronger effects on fluency, complexity, and self-efficacy than on accuracy or global proficiency. The third is an affective asymmetry, in which learners gain in enjoyment, well-being, and self-efficacy while teachers bear new costs in the form of AI-induced anxiety and monitoring workload. The fourth is a gap between individual adoption and institutional readiness, in which teachers and students are willing to use AI while the institutional structures that would make this use sustainable have not been built. The review argues that the positive impacts reported in the literature are real but conditional, produced in designed settings that most Iranian institutions have not yet created, and that closing this gap requires hybrid models of instruction, localized tools, AI literacy training that addresses the affective dimensions of adoption, and policy frameworks suited to under-resourced higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) uses three-dimensional information about a biological target to guide the identification and optimisation of small molecules. Molecular docking, virtual screening, molecular dynamics, free-energy calculations, and artificial-intelligence methods can help prioritise compounds for experimental testing. However, a plausible docking pose or favourable score is not proof of binding or therapeutic activity. Outcomes can be affected by protein structure quality, protonation, ligand preparation, receptor flexibility, scoring-function limitations, and the chemical space represented in a screening library. This narrative review presents a validation-first workflow: define a biologically justified target; assess the target structure and binding site; prepare proteins and ligands transparently; validate docking using reference ligands and appropriate controls; combine structural interpretation with complementary ranking; assess absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) risks; and confirm prioritised candidates experimentally. Recent AI-enabled methods are considered as tools for hypothesis generation rather than substitutes for medicinal chemistry judgement or laboratory evidence. The review also discusses reproducibility, uncertainty, and transparent reporting. The central recommendation is to connect every computational stage to a clear decision gate and to distinguish predictions from observations. This framework is intended to support student and early-stage research projects; it is not a report of new experimental data or a claim that any compound has been discovered.

Adjustability is a core determinant of ergonomic fit in office chairs, but its benefits depend on users being able to operate the controls and, on the chair, continuing to support the body as posture changes during work. We compared two high-end office chairs, the T90 (Sidiz; Chair A) and the Aeron (Herman Miller; Chair B), in two experiments to explore which design features may explain differences between them. In Experiment 1, 20 participants adjusted ten controls common to both chairs and rated perceived adjustment difficulty on four items. Chair A had significantly lower overall difficulty (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.008), with control-level advantages for headrest angle, armrest height, armrest rotation angle and lumbar support position; Chair B was easier for seat height, possibly because its side-mounted lever is more visible than Chair A's underside button. The headrest comparisons involved a third-party headrest fitted to Chair B, and control- and item-level tests were not corrected for multiple comparisons. In Experiment 2, the same participants completed a 15-minute multi-device task requiring repeated posture changes, reach and reorientation, then rated body-part discomfort, general comfort and satisfaction with five components. Discomfort and comfort did not differ; Chair A had higher satisfaction for the seat-pan and lumbar support (exploratory, uncorrected). Interviews suggested links to mechanism properties: Chair B's rear lumbar dial was often described as producing little perceptible change, and for controls without significant differences each chair appeared to leave a different aspect of the same need unmet. These findings suggest mechanical and interface properties that designers of adjustable office chairs may consider for dynamic, multi-device work.

Artificial intelligence (AI)–driven chatbots based on large language models are increasingly entering medical education, but evidence on the real-world use of domestic systems such as DeepSeek among Chinese medical interns is still scarce. This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence, patterns and perceptions of DeepSeek use among medical interns at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University. A total of 634 interns from clinical medicine, preventive medicine and nursing completed an anonymous questionnaire. Overall, about one-third of interns reported using DeepSeek. Among users, most engaged with the tool regularly, with over half using it several times per week. DeepSeek was primarily employed for completing assignments, searching for information, translation and polishing of written texts, while a smaller subset of users reported using it for data analysis. Attitudes toward DeepSeek were mainly neutral or optimistic, and across majors most users perceived its advantages and disadvantages as broadly balanced, while only a minority considered the disadvantages to outweigh the advantages. After adjustment, residence and major remained associated with DeepSeek use, whereas age and sex were not. Urban interns were more likely to report using DeepSeek than rural interns. Compared with clinical medicine interns, preventive medicine interns were less likely to report use, whereas nursing interns were more likely to do so. Among users, overall attitudes differed across majors, while usage frequency and the perceived balance of advantages and disadvantages did not. These findings provide descriptive evidence on the use and evaluation of DeepSeek among medical interns and may inform future institutional guidance on responsible use, verification of AI-generated information and academic integrity.

documents.abstract: As modern DRAM manufacturing processes continue to shrink, the Rowhammer vulnerability has emerged as one of the most severe threats to microarchitectural security isolation. To defend against such attacks, hardware vendors have introduced complex black-box defense mechanisms in memory controllers, such as FR-FCFS (First-Ready First-Come–First-Serve) queue coalescing, Target Row Refresh (TRR), and the open row policy. These defenses provide the context for this work; in the evaluation reported here, we explicitly model the FR-FCFS scheduling family and the open row policy, while realistic TRR is not modeled and is left for future work. These mechanisms have rendered traditional vulnerability exploitation approaches, which rely on security experts manually crafting inline assembly, increasingly unsustainable. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have become strong at software code generation. However, when applied to low-level hardware vulnerability exploitation, they encounter a severe “semantic–physical gap.” Conventional LLMs lack embodied cognition of physical hardware state machines; their generated memory access loops often compile and run correctly at the software layer, but the majority of requests are absorbed by caches and microarchitectural queues before reaching physical memory, trapping the LLM in a “false-positive state” where simulated ACT counts remain near zero. Most existing research treats LLMs as victims of Rowhammer attacks, overlooking their potential as active attack initiators at the hardware level. To address these challenges, this paper repurposes LLMs as microarchitectural attackers for the first time and designs AgentHammer—a closed-loop agent framework that allows LLMs to conduct automated hardware vulnerability exploitation. To bridge the software–hardware semantic gap, we construct a Hardware-Aware Simulation-in-the-Loop (HASIL) perception skill chain that deeply couples the QEMU full-system simulator with the Ramulator memory simulator. This chain captures low-level timing measurements—such as simulated ACT counts and simulated row conflict rates—transparently and reduces their dimensionality into natural language feedback comprehensible to LLMs. At the same time, we distill rigid low-level constraints—such as cache eviction and access stride—into reasoning primitives for the model, establishing a closed-loop verification pipeline of “perception, decision, feedback, and evolution,” in which the LLM adapts its parameters within the constraints set by human experts. Experimental results show that AgentHammer effectively breaks through the false-positive blind zone of pure software code generation. In complex microarchitectural simulation environments, the system autonomously reasons over low-level feedback logs and mutates parameters, successfully discovering, within our simulated configurations, the optimal access pattern that overcomes the FR-FCFS request-queue optimization and the open-row policy, ultimately achieving simulated row conflict. This work not only shows that large foundation models can explore physical boundaries in black-box environments through autonomous parameter adaptation, but also provides a basis for highly automated low-level hardware security assessment.

documents.abstract: Autonomous Multi-Material Self-Replicating Factory (AM-SRF) & Advanced Nuclear Micro-Battery Production for Deep-Space AI Infrastructure Abstract & System Overview The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence into deep space—specifically targeting the hostile, high-radiation environments of the Moon and Mars—demands an unprecedented paradigm shift in power generation, manufacturing autonomy, and resilience. Traditional silicon-based electronics and solar arrays fail under severe cosmic radiation, thermal fluctuations, and dust storms. To solve this, we introduce the Autonomous Multi-Material Self-Replicating Factory (AM-SRF), a unified single-module manufacturing system integrated with advanced isotope gas handling circuits, laser-assisted Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD), and poly-diamond nuclear micro-batteries. Powered by isotope-derived energy and resilient against planetary radiation, this infrastructure enables AI systems to construct their own habitats, manufacture industrial machinery, execute self-repair protocols, and harvest extraterrestrial resources such as helium-3. 1. Unified Single-Module Manufacturing Architecture (The "1-Machine" Concept) Unlike terrestrial multi-factory supply chains that rely on fragile logistics, the AM-SRF consolidates the entire production chain into a single, highly optimized growth and post-processing module. Isotope Gas Handling & Recirculation: The system features a closed-loop isotope recovery circuit connected to high-purity precursor gas tanks (such as \bm{98\%} enriched \bm{^{14}\text{CH}_4} or tritium-doped precursors). Mass flow controllers regulate gas delivery into a coaxial injection nozzle, while a recirculation pump and mixing valve capture unreacted gases, scrub impurities with clean \bm{\text{H}_2} carrier gas, and maintain optimal reaction pressures. Dynamic CVD Chamber: At the core of the machine is a hermetically sealed quartz and sapphire reaction chamber. A UV laser beam path, focused via high-precision lenses onto a rotating molybdenum disc substrate, drives layer-by-layer crystalline growth. In-Process Feedback & Laser Slicing: Automated optical probes and re-counter feedback mechanisms monitor layer uniformity and thickness in real time. Integrated laser cutting modules slice the grown crystalline boules into precise planar and spherical micro-battery arrays and structural components without breaking vacuum. 2. Advanced Material Science: Poly-Diamonds, Tritium, and Carbon-14 The operational longevity and radiation immunity of deep-space AI systems depend entirely on the material composition of their power sources and structural chassis. The AM-SRF produces batteries utilizing the following stacked material specifications: Transitional Layers (\bm{5\text{--}10\text{ nm}}): Single-crystal Carbon-14 (\bm{\text{sp}^3+\text{sp}^2} hybridization) providing exceptional p-type or n-type conductivity and atomic bonding integrity between the substrate and active cathode. Carbon-14 & Tritium Doped Diamond Cathodes (\bm{1\text{--}2\ \mu\text{m}}): Utilizing beta-voltaic conversion within a diamond lattice matrix. Diamond's wide bandgap (\bm{\sim5.5\text{ eV}}) and high displacement threshold energy make it impervious to radiation damage. Beta particles emitted by \bm{^{14}\text{C}} or tritium generate electron-hole pairs continuously for millennia without external recharging. Polyimide-Diamond Deposition Layers (\bm{10\text{--}20\ \mu\text{m}}): Polymer-matrix composite layers reinforced with carbon isotope doping, delivering superior mechanical strength, fracture toughness, and thermal dissipation. Substrates and Current Collectors: High-purity single-crystal diamond and copper-coated polymer substrates ensure efficient ion transport and ultra-low internal resistance, achieving energy densities exceeding \bm{2.60\text{ kW}\cdot\text{hr}/\text{cm}^3}. 3. Radiation Immunity and Deep-Space Survival Martian and lunar environments present lethal radiation hazards, including Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs) and Solar Particle Events (SPEs), which instantly degrade standard semiconductor architectures. Diamond Lattice Hardening: The nuclear micro-batteries and structural chassis produced by the AM-SRF utilize radiation-hardened diamond structures. Because carbon-14 and tritium beta decays are harnessed directly within the wide-bandgap diamond lattice, incoming external ionizing radiation is safely dissipated through collective lattice phonon interactions rather than generating destructive charge trapping. Self-Healing Electronic Substrates: The AI systems powered by these batteries operate within redundant fractal-wave network architectures. If micro-meteorite impacts or localized radiation spikes damage a circuit path, the AM-SRF's robotic manipulators and laser-cutting tools can instantly manufacture and swap replacement modules on the fly. 4. Autonomous City Construction and Self-Replication An AI governed by this infrastructure is not a passive tool, but an active planetary constructor. In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU): Using the AM-SRF's integrated regolith processing modules, the system extracts raw silicates, carbon, and metal oxides from lunar and Martian dust. Automated Scaling and Expansion: The factory uses its linear-rotary carrier tracks and multi-axis robotic arms to fabricate structural bricks, radiation-shielded habitats, solar-thermal mirrors, and additional CVD growth units. By replicating its own machinery, a single initial seed unit can expand into an industrial network capable of building entire subsurface cities and manufacturing plants autonomously. 5. Helium-3 Integration and Deep-Space Expansion As the AI colony expands its industrial footprint across the solar system, reliance on terrestrial-sourced isotopes transitions to abundant extraterrestrial resources. Transition to He-3 Fusion: The AM-SRF architecture is natively engineered to incorporate Helium-3 (\bm{^3\text{He}}) recovery and fusion energy integration. Lunar regolith, enriched with solar-wind-implanted helium-3 over billions of years, is harvested, thermally processed, and fed into advanced compact fusion reactors. Limitless Power for Deep Space: By shifting from beta-voltaic micro-batteries to localized He-3 fusion generators produced by the same self-replicating machinery, the AI obtains the massive energy throughput required for heavy manufacturing, atmospheric terraforming, and interstellar propulsion. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming teaching, learning and administration in higher education institutions (HEIs), yet responsibility for its governance is rarely assigned. This article develops and empirically tests the profile of an AI Manager for HEIs proposed by the Erasmus+ project FORCE AI. A literature-based definition and nine-area competence profile were examined in a sequential mixed-methods study, a survey of 387 students and staff from 13 countries and five nominal-group focus groups in Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Türkiye in 2025, which tested the elements stakeholders can rate: competences, responsibilities, placement, and qualifications. Only 17% of respondents knew of a designated AI-management responsibility at their institution; of the remainder, 71% considered one necessary and 76% expected an AI Manager to improve their experience. The expected mandate comprised training, ethical oversight, data security and strategy; preferences were split between a dedicated position and a shared cross-functional function. Survey respondents portrayed the role as a compliance-oriented technical specialist, whereas staff-dominated focus groups, rating the same competencies, prioritised leadership, change and project management, and communication alongside AI expertise and ethics; this contrast between methods and samples persists for staff respondents alone. The revised definition and profile position designated AI management, a dedicated AI Manager or a team with an accountable lead, as change leadership with technical credibility and give HEIs a tested basis for establishing this role.

Assessment preparation in teacher education remains a persistent concern as pre-service teachers are increasingly expected to design valid assessments, generate meaningful feedback, interpret learning evidence, and exercise professional judgment in AI-mediated classrooms. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of research on artificial intelligence-enhanced classroom assessment in pre-service teacher education from 2005 to 2025. Using Scopus-indexed publications, the study analyzed 344 documents from 242 sources to map publication trends, citation patterns, influential authors and institutions, geographic distribution, co-citation structures, keyword co-occurrence networks, and thematic evolution. Results show that the field is young but rapidly expanding, with an annual growth rate of 29.61% and a sharp increase in publications from 2022 onward, reflecting the growing influence of generative AI, ChatGPT, automated feedback, learning analytics, and intelligent learning systems. Co-citation analysis revealed three intellectual foundations: teacher knowledge and research foundations, generative AI-mediated pedagogical practice, formative feedback and automated assessment. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified four major thematic clusters: AI integration and ethical teacher education, intelligent learning systems and data-driven student learning, AI-supported feedback and personalization, and assessment analytics and evidence-based grading. The findings suggest that AI-enhanced classroom assessment is not merely a technological issue but a pedagogical and professional concern requiring assessment literacy, AI literacy, ethical judgment, and teacher agency. The study contributes a field-level understanding of this emerging research domain and highlights the need for more focused, ethical, and context-sensitive studies on how pre-service teachers design, evaluate, and use AI-supported classroom assessments.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is mostly used in education to generate solutions, provide feedback or support instruction; approaches that use AI outputs as objects of comparison and reflection remain less explored. This small-scale exploratory qualitative case study examined AI-supported comparative reflection in sustainability-oriented mathematical modelling. Twelve pre-service mathematics teachers individually developed models for a task on water use in a school garden and then compared them with a model produced by ChatGPT (GPT-4o), reflecting on the comparison in writing. Modelling products, written comparisons and reflection forms were analysed using inductive content analysis. The comparison prompted participants to question assumptions, identify limitations in both models and consider alternative variables and representations; most described how they would revise their models. Their accounts contained indications of critical, creative and metacognitive reasoning. However, several participants treated the AI output as an answer key, some of their critiques echoed weaknesses that the AI had listed about itself, and none noticed a computational inconsistency deliberately retained in the output. As the design included no comparison condition or pre–post measure, the findings describe patterns of reasoning displayed during the activity, not improvements in thinking skills or modelling competence. Implications for teacher education are discussed.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have intensified debates about automation, authorship, and labour across creative industries. Yet these discussions are often dominated by disruption and replacement narratives, leaving limited attention to how creators interpret and negotiate AI in everyday practice, particularly in non-Western contexts. This paper examines how Social Cartoon Influencers (SCIs) in Vietnam interpret and use GenAI within their routine creative production. The study combines semi-structured interviews and contextual observations of production workflows through the lens of AI imaginaries. Findings reveal that creators position AI as a creative assistant rather than a co-author, using it for ideation, optimisation and routine tasks, while reserving final authorship for humans. The clear human-AI boundary results from concerns surrounding situated notions of authenticity and ‘national tone’. The paper argues that AI adoption is shaped by negotiated boundaries around authorship, authenticity, and cultural legitimacy.

documents.abstract: Additional production does not translate automatically into household income. This working paper presents a reproducible accounting framework for tracing a stated AI-related production scenario through capital consumption, cross-border income, corporate saving, taxes and transfers to resident income and household groups. Australia was the first implementation. This United States application examines the framework under different institutional arrangements, including substantial income from abroad, retained corporate profits and pension-income attribution. It uses US Bureau of Economic Analysis sources and selected scenario settings from the Yale Budget Lab’s AI-Fiscal project. It does not replicate the Budget Lab’s tax model. The contribution is an explicit, inspectable measurement protocol: definitions and equations specify the required inputs; accounting checks reconcile the flows; and evidence labels distinguish reported observations, derived quantities, assumptions and unidentified results. Missing evidence is not silently replaced with zero. In four selected Moderate cases using a 2025 base, with government retaining additional revenue, household income ranges from USD 25.20 to USD 49.32 per USD 100 of additional production. Net resident income ranges from USD 55.96 to USD 82.62 per USD 100 of additional production. These differences illustrate the consequences of source factor-share assumptions and alternative foreign-income responses. They are selected conditional cases, not confidence intervals or estimates of realised US AI gains. The specification preserves the annual illustration using 2023 household component proxies. A separately dated application uses provisional 2024 group proxies and runs Q2 2026 conditional cases with explicitly carried-forward annual recipient ratios. These applications are not a time series of measured AI effects. The empirical real net dividend per person remains unidentified. Editorial release 0.3.1 preserves the computational core and dated application unchanged while clarifying definitions, fiscal labels, aggregation, rounding and presentation. The deposit includes an expert summary, mathematical specification, latest-data report, executable replication package and verification receipt. ChatGPT assisted development and internal verification; Claude was used for separate AI-assisted audits of earlier work. Independent human scientific validation remains outstanding. Research and release responsibility rests with Muhammad Imran Khan, acting in a personal capacity; no employer or institutional endorsement is implied. Author-owned documents and results are licensed under CC BY 4.0; code is MIT-licensed. Third-party materials retain their own terms. Readers should begin with the one-page expert summary. Feedback is particularly welcome on the scenario-to-national-accounts mapping, institutional boundaries and evidence needed to establish marginal household incidence. documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence changes both the skills used at work and the conditions under which employment decisions are made. Awareness of these changes does not necessarily coincide with confidence in adapting a career. This study examines that distinction in 385 adult, AI-aware survey records from Bangladesh, including 238 law students and 61 respondents classified as law graduates. Five statements separately assess awareness of workplace rights and responsibilities, recognition of protection from unfair automated decisions, reported complementary skill development, adaptation confidence and the perceived preparedness benefit of understanding labour issues. Analyses combine full response distributions, joint endorsement patterns, paired comparisons, ordinal correlations and an exploratory proportional-odds model. Recognition of the need for protection was endorsed by 79.2%, compared with 48.8% endorsing adaptation confidence, a paired difference of 30.4 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval 23.9–36.6). General rights awareness and skill development had small positive ordinal associations with confidence. In the adjusted ordinal model, their odds ratios were 1.30 (95% interval 1.04–1.61; Holm p = 0.038) and 1.40 (1.09–1.79; Holm p = 0.024) respectively. The protection-recognition estimate was less certain, although the two awareness coefficients were not demonstrably different. The findings distinguish rights recognition, reported action and confidence rather than establish a causal awareness-to-adaptability pathway. They support evaluating legal-literacy education alongside practical career tasks and institutional safeguards. The mixed sample, study-specific single items, undocumented recruitment and fieldwork dates, and source-documentation limitations constrain inference. A subsequent study should use verified graduate eligibility, independent legal-knowledge assessments and longitudinal career outcomes.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in speech and language therapy (SLT). Evidence on SLTs’ attitudes towards it has been largely descriptive, generated with study-specific questionnaires or with validated attitude scales analysed descriptively. The psychological factors associated with those attitudes have recently been examined among undergraduate students in the profession, but not among clinicians in practice. Aims: To examine whether AI literacy and AI anxiety are independently associated with attitudes towards AI beyond prior AI use, self-directed AI learning and formal AI training, and whether the two are differentially related to the positive and negative dimensions of those attitudes. Methods & Procedures: A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 180 SLTs in Türkiye, recruited by convenience and predominantly early in their careers (mean age 25.4 years), using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale and the General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS). Hierarchical multiple regressions were complemented by comparisons of each construct’s correlations and adjusted coefficients across the two attitude dimensions, sensitivity analyses and post hoc confirmatory factor analyses. Outcomes & Results: Beyond the experiential variables, AI literacy and AI anxiety explained an additional 15.2% of the variance in positive attitudes, with AI literacy the only independent correlate (β = .403, p < .001), and an additional 42.1% of the variance in attitudes towards AI-related drawbacks (reverse-scored, so that higher values indicate fewer concerns), with anxiety the only independent correlate (β = −.679, p < .001). Each construct was significantly more strongly associated with one dimension than with the other, in both zero-order correlations and adjusted coefficients (all p ≤ .001). None of the AI-related experiential variables remained significant. The pattern held across sensitivity analyses, in which one year or more of professional experience was also associated with more positive attitudes. Absolute fit was poor for the GAAIS and AI literacy measurement models and mixed for the AI anxiety model. Conclusions & Implications: In a predominantly early-career, private-sector sample of Turkish SLTs, self-reported AI literacy and AI anxiety were differentially associated with attitudes towards AI, each related primarily to a different attitude dimension. These patterns require cautious interpretation, because the anxiety and negative-attitude measures, although empirically distinguishable, share item content and substantial variance, and because the literacy measure indexes general rather than clinically situated competence. AI literacy and AI-related concerns may still be complementary targets for education supporting clinically responsible integration of AI into SLT.

documents.abstract: Unexpected equipment stoppages can interrupt production, increase maintenance costs and reduce manufacturing consistency. This paper presents a low-cost Internet of Things (IoT) prototype for machine-condition monitoring as a foundation for predictive maintenance in smart factories. The prototype uses an ESP32 microcontroller connected to a DHT22 temperature-and-humidity sensor, an SW-420 digital vibration detector and an ACS712 current-sensor module. A low-voltage DC motor is driven through an L298N module, while LEDs and a buzzer provide local threshold-based indications. The ESP32 periodically sends a JSON payload over Wi-Fi to a FastAPI service hosted on a Mac computer. The backend exposes endpoints for receiving the latest sensor data and retrieving historical records, which are stored in an SQLite database. A Streamlit dashboard displays the latest measurements and supports historical visualization. During implementation, sensor readings were visible through the serial monitor, the HTTP POST request returned status code 200, and the history endpoint returned stored records. These observations demonstrate the operation of the core data pipeline. The current prototype performs monitoring and rule-based alerts; a trained and validated artificial-intelligence model has not yet been implemented. In addition, the current field from the ACS712 represents a raw analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) reading rather than calibrated amperes. Future work includes sensor calibration, longer-term data collection, fault-labelled experiments, anomaly detection, and validation of machine-learning methods against documented operating conditions.

Agriculture is essential in economic growth and food availability, particularly in India, where a significant percentage of the population depends on farming for their livelihoods. However, agricultural communities encounter various difficulties, such as climate variability, irregular rainfall, soil degradation, water scarcity, and fluctuating market prices. Traditional crop selection methods often depend on traditional knowledge and traditional farming methods, which may may not sufficiently consider variations in environmental factors and market demands. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based intelligent crop selection system that combines environmental parameters and economic and market indicators to improve farming decisions. The developed framework examines important environmental variables, including soil nutrient content, temperature, humidity, rainfall, and soil pH, together with financial indicators such as market demand for crops, market price, and expected economic returns. ML-based predictive techniques, including Random Forest, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), are developed and assessed for crop prediction and recommendation. The system is designed to determine appropriate crop varieties by considering environmental compatibility and economic potential, providing farmers with recommendations based on analytical data rather than relying solely on conventional crop selection techniques. The experimental evaluation compares the predictive performance of the implemented models and identifies an appropriate model for crop recommendation. By integrating environmental suitability with market analysis, the proposed approach seeks to improve crop selection, optimize agricultural resource use, reduce cultivation risks, and improve farmers' financial returns for farmers. The system can also be extended through Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and cloud computing to enable real-time environmental monitoring and scalable agricultural applications. This approach contributes to precision agriculture by combining machine learning-based prediction with environmental and economic analysis to promote sustainable farming practices and informed agricultural decision-making.

documents.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a problem that will be very hard to deal with globally in public health, but most AI (Artificial Intelligence) solutions for AD prediction are still based on neuroimaging methods (e.g., MRI and PET) that are very expensive. This restricts the use of AI for monitoring at the population level. Hence, there is a need for predictive frameworks that can rely on public health data, which are available in tabular format, to forecast the trends of diseases like AD affecting the population. In this research, we put forward a Dual-Stream Hybrid Ensemble Framework for the adoption of Alzheimer's disease predictive methods by longitudinal CDC data (2015–2022). The research works on checking the ability of modern deep learning architectures to outperform the strong Gradient Boosting Machine baselines on complex epidemiological tabular datasets. The framework consists of a Feature Tokenizer Transformer (FT-Transformer) joined with three leading GBMs (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) and a deep Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). To maintain the validity of the scientific findings, we impose a strict “Chinese Wall” feature segregation rule to avoid data leakage by disabling the use of context-specific proxy identifiers in the binary classification stream. Furthermore, Probability Target Encoding and Cost-Sensitive Learning methods are put into practice to tackle high-cardinality categorical features and severe class imbalance issues (~1:9.5). The outcomes of the experiments indicate that the FT-Transformer provides the best regression performance with an R-squared value of 0.9451, while XGBoost gives a lower value of 0.8752, and the final weighted regression ensemble provides an R-squared value of 0.9394. For classification under leakage constraints, the cost-sensitive ensemble reaches high sensitivity at the cost of precision at Recall = 89.75%, thereby indicating a demonstrates utility for identifying AD/SCD-related surveillance strata even though metadata proxies have been removed. To sum it up, the new research results give empirical evidence that deep learning by transformers can outperform classic boosting methods for public health monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease if the right tokenization and training restrictions are applied.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) supports environmental performance prediction and the evaluation of alternatives in architectural design. However, improvements in energy or carbon indicators alone do not demonstrate that non-human life holds independent value in design decisions. This chapter examines AI and related computational design approaches in architecture from an ecocentric perspective through a focused narrative review and conceptual synthesis supported by a structured database search. The 375 raw records retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science were reduced to 256 unique records; following title and abstract screening, a final purposive selection of 19 studies was established. Together with one supplementary publication, the 20 documents were examined under the themes of performance and decision-making, life cycle boundaries, the representation of non-human life, habitat geometry and materials, time and maintenance, and visual generation and ecological validation. The synthesis informs a preliminary ecocentric assessment framework comprising three dimensions: stakeholder scope, integration of environmental and ecological impacts into decision-making, and ecological responsibility. By distinguishing computational success from ecological outcomes, the framework provides an analytical basis for examining who benefits from design decisions, how environmental and ecological requirements influence those decisions, and how responsibility for their outcomes is addressed.

Abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have substantially influenced artificial intelligence by enabling computational systems to learn representations from images, language, behavioural sequences, and other complex data. This paper presents a selective narrative review of their conceptual development, applications, evaluation requirements, and societal implications. It synthesises foundational and application-oriented publications concerning computer vision, natural language processing, healthcare image classification, financial prediction, cybersecurity, and reinforcement learning. The review uses a qualitative comparative framework to examine the task addressed, the evidence reported, and the conditions limiting interpretation. The reviewed literature illustrates the value of learned representations and task-specific architectures, while also showing why benchmark performance cannot alone establish operational reliability or social benefit. Cross-cutting concerns include data quality, distribution shift, interpretability, subgroup disparities, adversarial vulnerability, privacy, and computational requirements. The paper proposes a practical evaluation framework connecting task suitability, data provenance, appropriate baselines, external validation, human oversight, and monitoring after deployment. No new model training, expert interviews, public-opinion survey, or pooled statistical analysis is reported. The synthesis concludes that the contribution of ANNs should be assessed through performance under relevant operating conditions and the consequences of their use, rather than through accuracy alone. Keywords: artificial neural networks; artificial intelligence; deep learning; representation learning; model evaluation; responsible AI.

The construction industry continues to encounter considerable inefficiencies associated with the manual interpretation and processing of heterogeneous cost estimation documentation, which is characterised by a paucity of background data. The present study puts forward a Large Language Model (LLM)-based framework for the automated recognition, semantic structuring, and enrichment of construction cost estimates originating from unstandardised Excel spreadsheets. The proposed framework uses a combination of domain-specific data annotation, machine learning-assisted document understanding and semantic similarity retrieval to convert semi-structured procurement and estimation documents into standardised, machine-readable datasets. A large corpus of historical construction estimates was collected, organised and manually labelled to create a training dataset for the LLM-based recognition pipeline. An API-oriented architecture automatically parses, classifies and converts uploaded spreadsheets into structured entities, including estimate positions, quantities, units, unit costs and total costs. The framework also incorporates a semantic similarity matching mechanism that compares newly uploaded estimates with historical priced estimates stored in the reference database. Consequently, the system can automatically suggest historically relevant unit prices and related CO₂ indicators for similar construction positions. Experimental validation has demonstrated that the proposed framework achieves a semantic position-matching accuracy of over 85%, enabling the automatic completion of 50–70% of newly uploaded estimates. Furthermore, the solution reduces the effort required for manual estimation by around 70% compared to traditional workflows. The findings suggest that using LLM-assisted recognition and historical knowledge retrieval can substantially improve the productivity, consistency and sustainability of construction cost management and procurement processes.

Animal communication takes place via vocalizations, body posture, movement, facial expressions, and context. Although there are some animal communications known to humans, decoding the internal state of an animal correctly may be challenging, especially if there are different species of animals. An idea of an AI Animal Translator is introduced in this paper. It is supposed that the system would perform audio analysis, computer vision, machine learning, and other context-related operations to classify the animals' sounds and behaviour into understandable human messages like hunger, fear, pain, stress, comfort, alertness, or any social activity. The proposed system would include data collection, preprocessing, features extraction, multimodal classification, confidence assessment, and alerting for users. This device should be used as an auxiliary system to help people to better comprehend animals' communication, but not as a direct translation from one language to another. The review of related scientific trends, the problem statement, the architecture of the proposed system, evaluation methodology, applications, limitations, ethical considerations, and further research are covered in the paper.

Introduction This scoping review aims to evaluate artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, for predicting periodontal risks in orthodontic patients and to identify methodological gaps limiting clinical translation. Methods Reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR and PRISMA-S guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across six electronic databases (PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library), grey literature, and citation tracking (Jan 1, 2018–June 1, 2025). Out of 880 identified records (312 duplicates removed; 568 screened), 56 full texts were evaluated, yielding 3 core clinical CBCT studies meeting strict eligibility criteria (Xu et al., 2024; Pirayesh et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Methodological quality and risk of bias were appraised using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results Reported performance for orthodontically induced inflammatory root resorption (OIIRR) ranged from 82.1% accuracy in small canine-induced resorption cohorts to >94% accuracy in larger grading frameworks. However, critical appraisal revealed a high risk of bias across all studies due to single-center retrospective designs, lack of independent external validation, and missing calibration metrics. Direct clinical evidence for AI prediction of gingival recession or orthodontic alveolar bone loss was insufficient within strict pre-cutoff parameters. Discussion While AI demonstrates technical feasibility for assessing orthodontically related root resorption risk, robust individual-level risk prediction remains unestablished. Prospective multicenter external validation and adherence to standardized reporting guidelines are required prior to routine clinical adoption.

Digital transformation is becoming a crucial driver for innovating operational models in the postal logistics sector.The robust growth of e-commerce, the digital economy, and the increasing demands for speed and service quality have created an urgent need for logistics enterprises to apply digital technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data, cloud computing, and automation.In Vietnam, the digital transformation in the postal logistics industry has achieved some results; however, there are still many limitations in technological infrastructure, data connectivity, human resources, and the level of technology adoption among enterprises.Based on the synthesis and analysis of domestic and international specialised studies and reports, this research evaluates the current status of applying digital transformation technology in the postal logistics sector in Vietnam.Simultaneously, it proposes development orientations and solutions according to the roadmap to 2030 and the vision to 2045.Digital transformation not only improves operational efficiency and reduces logistics costs but also lays the foundation for building a smart postal logistics ecosystem that meets the development requirements of the digital economy.

This study explored the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in chemistry instruction, focusing on teachers’ utilization patterns, perceptions, and the challenges they encounter. A sample of 18 chemistry teachers from various institutions participated, providing insights into the types and frequency of AI tools used, including ChatGPT, ChemCollective, and PhET Interactive Simulations. Findings indicate that generative AI tools—particularly ChatGPT—are the most widely adopted due to their accessibility, versatility, and ease of integration. In contrast, subject-specific and creative AI platforms remain underutilized, suggesting that familiarity, perceived complexity, and awareness significantly influence adoption patterns. Teachers demonstrated strongly positive perceptions of AI integration in both curriculum and instruction, recognizing its potential to enhance content delivery, student engagement, personalized learning, and the development of 21st-century skills. No significant differences were found across institutions, indicating a shared readiness to integrate AI in chemistry education. Despite these favorable perceptions, effective implementation is constrained by technical limitations, infrastructure gaps, data quality concerns, usability challenges, ethical issues, and privacy risks. Teachers also expressed concerns about over-reliance on AI and the potential reduction of meaningful teacher–student interaction, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a balanced, human-centered approach. Overall, the findings support the strategic and guided adoption of AI as a pedagogical enhancement tool rather than a substitute for professional judgment and instructional expertise. The results highlight the need for structured, discipline-specific professional development that emphasizes prompt literacy, critical evaluation of AI outputs, ethical awareness, and pedagogical alignment. Strengthening technological infrastructure, establishing sustained institutional support systems, and developing clear guidelines for responsible AI use are essential to ensure effective, equitable, and ethically grounded integration of AI in chemistry education.

documents.abstract: Commercial banks in Kenya have invested heavily in artificial intelligence (AI), yet sector profitability has weakened, with average return on assets (ROA) falling from 3.3 percent in 2021 to 2.6 percent in 2024. This research investigated the effect of AI adoption on the financial performance of commercial banks in Kenya. Specifically, it examined the effects of AI-enabled customer service, machine learning credit scoring, robotic process automation and AI-driven fraud detection on financial performance, measured by ROA, as well as the mediating effect of operational efficiency and the moderating effect of bank size. A census of all 38 commercial banks licensed by the Central Bank of Kenya was undertaken, using data from audited annual reports and Central Bank of Kenya supervisory returns. Data were analysed using random effects panel regression with cluster-robust standard errors, the causal steps approach supplemented by the Sobel test, and moderated regression. AI-enabled customer service had a positive and significant effect on ROA (β = 0.927, p = 0.003). Machine learning credit scoring (β = −0.046, p = 0.841), robotic process automation (β = −0.450, p = 0.098) and AI-driven fraud detection (β = 0.137, p = 0.459) had no significant effects. AI-enabled customer service lowered the cost-to-income ratio (β = −0.194, p < 0.001), but operational efficiency did not significantly mediate its relationship with ROA (Sobel z = 1.287, p = 0.198). The interaction between AI adoption and bank size was not significant (β = 0.154, p = 0.589). The study concluded that the effect of AI adoption on bank performance is application-specific. Only customer-facing AI translated into higher profitability, while the credit scoring, process automation and fraud detection applications did not. Operational efficiency did not mediate, and bank size did not moderate, the connection between AI adoption and performance.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming tourism destinations through personalized services, conversational and generative interfaces, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making. Yet technology adoption alone does not explain how destinations convert AI-generated information into coordinated managerial action. Objective: This study addresses that organizational problem through a conceptual integrative review of research on AI-enabled tourism services, smart destination management, destination governance, visitor experience, organizational capabilities, workforce readiness, and responsible data practices. Methods: The synthesis identifies four interconnected application domains: AI-driven personalization, conversational and generative visitor interaction, predictive visitor-flow analytics, and data-driven destination governance. These domains are abstracted into the AI-Enabled Smart Destination Management (AI-SDM) framework, which connects AI-Enabled Service Capability, Smart Destination Governance Capability, and Visitor Experience Outcomes. Results: Visitor and operational intelligence functions as the principal conversion input, while visitor-generated behavioral and experiential feedback supports subsequent organizational learning and AI adaptation. Workforce AI Readiness and Responsible Data Governance are positioned as enabling conditions. The framework contributes to destination-management theory by shifting attention from AI adoption toward the organizational capability required to sense relevant visitor information, interpret and coordinate responses, and responsibly convert intelligence into destination action and visitor value. It complements broad smart-tourism and emerging cognitive-destination architectures by specifying the organizational intelligence-to-action mechanism that links AI-enabled interactions with destination governance and learning. Conclusion: The paper concludes with propositions and an empirical research agenda for measurement development and validation.
